questions.q: Which README order best serves a busy reviewer?
options: Problem, approach, findings, how to run it
Installation details, then license, then a long history
Only a list of libraries
Personal biography first, project last
questions.explain: The README should state the problem and result quickly, then show the approach and how to reproduce it.

questions.q: You accidentally committed an API key and then deleted it in the next commit. What should you do?
options: Nothing, the deletion fixed it
Rename the repository
Add a comment to the README
Revoke or rotate the key and treat it as compromised
questions.explain: The key remains in git history after a later commit removes it, so it must be revoked or rotated.

questions.q: Your capstone data is fictional. How should the repository handle that?
options: Present results as if from a real company
Disclose clearly in the README that the data is fictional or synthetic
Remove the data description
Claim the data is confidential
questions.explain: Disclosing synthetic data keeps your portfolio honest and avoids misleading reviewers.

questions.q: Which is generally the better portfolio strategy?
options: Twenty unfinished repositories
One giant repository with everything
Three or four well-documented projects, pinned
Only private repositories
questions.explain: A few clear, documented projects are easier to review than a large pile of unfinished work.

questions.q: Why pin library versions and set random seeds?
options: It makes the model more accurate
It lets a reader rerun and reproduce your results
It hides your code from others
It is required by GitHub
questions.explain: Pinned versions and seeds make results reproducible, which builds trust in your work.
